methodological_rigor.justification: Retrospective single-center cohort at the University Hospital of Brasilia (2014-2021) of 262 CRC patients (193 <70; 62/69 ≥70 - the text is inconsistent) comparing outcomes by age group. Appropriate exclusion of emergency surgeries, hereditary syndromes, and synchronous tumors to isolate elective curative-intent surgery. Statistical approach is reasonable (Poisson with robust variance for PRs, cumulative logistic for ordinal stage, Cox PH with stepwise covariate selection using p<0.25 entry threshold). Limitations: single-center, healthy-survivor selection bias explicitly acknowledged, short follow-up, combined colon + rectal tumors, no formal geriatric/frailty assessment, and only three comorbidities captured (HTN, DM, ASA). Stage IV survival difference (p=0.0468, n=37) is highlighted but noted as underpowered. There is inconsistent reporting of the ≥70 group size (both 62 and 69 appear in the manuscript).

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The finding that chronological age alone does not independently predict OS/DFS in carefully selected elderly CRC patients is clinically useful and reinforces SIOG-aligned guidance to use physiologic status rather than age for surgical decisions. The Brazilian single-center real-world data add context for middle-income settings. Clinical impact is tempered by selection bias and short follow-up. Oxford LoE is 4 for a retrospective single-center cohort.

reporting_quality.justification: Observational cohort should follow STROBE; adherence is not explicitly claimed but most STROBE items are present (eligibility, data sources, variables, statistical methods, limitations, bias discussion). Tables 1-6 and Figures 1-2 are referenced. IRB approval and ethics protocol number are provided. Discrepancy between N=62 and N=69 for the elderly group between abstract and results introduces a reporting inconsistency. No data or code availability statement is provided.

novelty_literature.justification: The core finding that age alone is not an independent survival predictor after adjustment is well-established in the CRC literature (Mima 2020, Aquina 2017, Brouwer 2019, SIOG 2013), and the authors cite these extensively. The novel contribution is setting-specific (Brazilian tertiary center) rather than conceptually new. The paradox of earlier-stage disease in elderly surgical candidates is plausibly a selection bias finding rather than a new biological insight.

writing_presentation.justification: Manuscript is generally organized with clear section headings, a comprehensive discussion, and appropriate cross-referencing of tables/figures. However, there are noticeable grammatical and syntactic issues ('169 (73.6%) were younger... and 62 (26.3%) were 70 years or older' contradicts abstract n=69; 'demonstrate that age-based treatment decisions should be informed...' starting with a lowercase verb; 'T presents as T1 + T2'). Discussion is somewhat repetitive. Adequate but not polished.

key_strengths: Restriction to elective curative-intent surgery to isolate age effect from emergency/presentation confounding
Use of Poisson with robust variance, cumulative logistic, and Cox PH with structured covariate entry
Explicit discussion of healthy-survivor selection bias as a core interpretive frame
Real-world middle-income setting (Brazil) adds geographic breadth to an otherwise high-income-heavy literature
Comprehensive assessment across epidemiological, surgical, pathological, and oncological dimensions
key_concerns: Inconsistent reporting of the elderly group size (N=69 in abstract vs N=62 in results)
Single-center retrospective design with short/variable follow-up and no external validation
No formal geriatric/frailty assessment despite being the central thesis
Core finding is largely confirmatory of existing SIOG-aligned literature
Combined colon and rectal tumors limits site-specific inference
No data/code availability and no reporting-checklist claim
chief_reviewer.rationale: A competent but incremental single-center retrospective study with notable internal inconsistency and modest novelty; best fit is a lower-tier oncology journal with major revisions to reconcile the N discrepancy and strengthen methods.
